newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels advance in absence of Zaire peace deal.
newsitem.headline: Rebels advance in absence of Zaire peace deal.

text.p: Rebels were advancing on Zaire's capital of Kinshasa on Monday after President Mobutu Sese Seko refused to bow to a demand by their leader, Laurent Kabila, for his immediate resignation.
South Africa's President Nelson Mandela said fresh talks would take place within eight to 10 days after the three men met on a South African ship but failed to broker a deal.
Kabila said his forces, reported by residents to be within 100 km (60 miles) of Kinshasa, would move on the capital while Mobutu considered the rebel demand.
Church sources said the rebels reached their new positions in one day, advancing from their previous forward base at Kenge, 200 km (125 miles) from the teeming city of five million people.

A South African official said Mobutu's offer to hand over to an elected president was rejected, but mediators would be working in the next few days on a way for him to cede power to a transitional authority.

"The understanding is that Mr Kabila will want to lead that transitional authority," the official, who would not be named, said on board the converted icebreaker SAS Outeniqua. The idea was not to humiliate Mobutu, he said.
Kabila told Reuters by telephone from the ship in Congo's port of Pointe Noire: "If we make it to Kinshasa before the eight days then too bad but we cannot wait while he (Mobutu) makes up his mind."
Kabila, 56, was reported to be headed late on Sunday for his stronghold at Zaire's second city of Lubumbashi, the rear base for the offensive against Kinshasa.

U.N. officials in Kisangani said at least 100 Rwandan Hutu refugees were crushed to death in a train while on their way to being airlifted home. Hundreds were reported injured, with more than 50 of them in serious condition.
"I think this is one of the most horrifying events I have ever seen in all my years as an aid worker," said Kilian Kleinschmidt, head of the Kisangani office of the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR.

Aid workers and journalists saw dozens of bodies tumbling from six open wagons as the train pulled into Kisangani station. Survivors leapt over the sides as the train completed its a two-hour journey from Biaro camp 41 km (25 miles) away.

Some rebel sources in Kisangani said his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) would delay the final push on Kinshasa until a rebel force of 10,000 to 12,000 troops had assembled near the capital.
At Lubumbashi international airport, hundreds of rebel soldiers boarded planes taking them to the front lines.
Troops from the United States, the former colonial power Belgium, France and Britain were waiting in Congo, across the river from Kinshasa, to evacuate Western nationals in the event of trouble.
The rebels have won control of about three quarters of Zaire in just seven months of fighting and are moving forward on several fronts.
Kabila's lightning rebellion has all but broken Mobutu's three-decade hold on power over the mineral rich state at the heart of Africa.

Mobutu, 66, now enfeebled by prostate cancer, used guile and cunning to dominate Zaire by buying off his political enemies and winning Cold War support from the United States as a bulwark against Soviet communist expansion.
Zaire accuses neighbours Uganda, Rwanda and Angola, antagonised in the past by Mobutu, of supporting Kabila's military effort. All three deny involvement.
